messages.subject: specific objectivity & adaptive testing
parts:
Hi Phil,

 

I am currently working on an adaptive intelligence test.

I always thought that specific objectivity or sample independence is a necessary condition for adaptive testing,

because only if the rank of the item difficulty is the same for all respondents independent of ability, and

the rank of the person ability is the same for items independently of difficulty,

it does not matter which item of the item pool is used.

 

But there are a lot of books and papers describing a 2PL or 3PL adaptive test.

So my question is: How do I argue that. Why am I allowed to use a 2PL or 3PL?

 

Many thanks for your help.

Best regards, Bruno

messages.subject: Re: specific objectivity & adaptive testing
parts:
On Sat, Aug 5, 2017 at 9:31 AM, <bruno....@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Phil,

 

I am currently working on an adaptive intelligence test.

I always thought that specific objectivity or sample independence is a necessary condition for adaptive testing,

because only if the rank of the item difficulty is the same for all respondents independent of ability, and

the rank of the person ability is the same for items independently of difficulty,

it does not matter which item of the item pool is used.

 

But there are a lot of books and papers describing a 2PL or 3PL adaptive test.

So my question is: How do I argue that. Why am I allowed to use a 2PL or 3PL?

Sample independence is something that should hold for all IRT models, though specific objectivity only for Rasch models. I personally find specific objectively more of a buzz-word than something practically useful. 

When fitting statistical models to empirical data, we generally want models that reflect the properties of the data, which Rasch models often will not accomplish (e.g., accounting for guessing, noticing that some items seem to separate lower/higher individuals better than others, including information about the distractor items, etc). Ignoring these properties can lead to improper inferences about the latent traits, which is generally why more flexible response models are used in practice. 

That's not to say you couldn't build a CAT with just Rasch items. Doing so means that you are selecting items that match the latent ability right at the inflection points, which in this case is identical to picking items with "maximum information" given some provisional ability estimate. From a CAT perspective though, we're typically more interested in building realistic adaptive tests that reflect empirical properties inherent in testing situations rather than building some situation specific (and largely unverifiable) specific objectivity measure. HTH. 

Phil

Many thanks for your help.

Best regards, Bruno
